Multithreading and Concurrency.explanation: Multithreading allows a Java program to execute multiple tasks concurrently by using multiple threads. Concurrency helps improve responsiveness, resource utilization, and performance when tasks can be performed independently or overlap in execution.

Introduction to Threads.explanation: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a program. Java allows multiple threads to run concurrently, enabling different tasks to execute independently.
Introduction to Threads.example: A web application can use separate threads to handle multiple client requests.
points_to_remember: A thread represents an independent path of execution.
Every Java program starts with at least one main thread.
Threads can execute tasks concurrently.
Use start() to begin a new thread.

Creating Threads.explanation: Java provides multiple ways to create threads. The common approaches are extending the Thread class and implementing the Runnable interface.
Creating Threads.example: A background task such as file processing can be executed in a separate thread.
points_to_remember: Override the run() method to define thread behavior.
Call start() instead of directly calling run().
Calling start() creates a new execution path.
Runnable is generally more flexible than extending Thread.

Thread Lifecycle.explanation: A thread moves through different states during its lifetime. Java defines states such as NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and TERMINATED.
Thread Lifecycle.example: A thread is NEW before start(), RUNNABLE while executing, and TERMINATED after completing execution.
points_to_remember: NEW means the thread has been created but not started.
RUNNABLE means the thread is ready or running.
WAITING means the thread is waiting indefinitely.
TERMINATED means the thread has completed execution.

Thread Methods.explanation: The Thread class provides methods for controlling and monitoring thread execution.
Thread Methods.example: join() can be used when one thread must wait for another thread to finish.
points_to_remember: start() starts a thread.
run() contains the task performed by the thread.
join() waits for another thread to finish.
sleep() pauses the current thread for a specified duration.
isAlive() checks whether a thread is still running.

Thread Priority.explanation: Thread priority provides a scheduling hint to the JVM about the relative importance of threads. Java priorities range from 1 to 10.
Thread Priority.example: A developer may assign different priorities as scheduling hints, although execution order should not be assumed.
points_to_remember: Minimum priority is 1.
Normal priority is 5.
Maximum priority is 10.
Thread priority does not guarantee execution order.

Synchronization.explanation: Synchronization controls access to shared resources so that multiple threads do not modify shared data at the same time in an unsafe way.
Synchronization.example: Synchronization can protect a shared counter from simultaneous modifications by multiple threads.
points_to_remember: Synchronization helps protect shared mutable data.
The synchronized keyword provides mutual exclusion.
Only one thread can execute a synchronized method on the same object at a time.
Excessive synchronization can reduce concurrency.

Race Condition.explanation: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the program result depends on the timing or order of thread execution.
Race Condition.example: Two threads incrementing the same counter without synchronization can produce an unexpected result.
points_to_remember: Race conditions involve shared mutable state.
The result can depend on thread timing.
Synchronization or concurrency utilities can help prevent race conditions.
Race conditions can be difficult to reproduce and debug.

Inter-Thread Communication.explanation: Inter-thread communication allows threads to coordinate their work. Java provides wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() for communication between threads using an object's monitor.
Inter-Thread Communication.example: A consumer thread can wait until a producer thread has made data available.
points_to_remember: wait() releases the object's monitor while waiting.
notify() wakes one waiting thread.
notifyAll() wakes all waiting threads.
wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() must be used while holding the object's monitor.

Executor Framework.explanation: The Executor Framework provides higher-level APIs for managing and executing tasks using thread pools instead of manually creating individual threads.
Executor Framework.example: A server can use a thread pool to process multiple tasks without creating a new thread for every request.
points_to_remember: ExecutorService manages a pool of threads.
submit() schedules tasks for execution.
Thread pools can reduce thread creation overhead.
Call shutdown() when the executor is no longer needed.

Callable and Future.explanation: Callable represents a task that can return a result and throw an exception. Future represents the result of an asynchronous computation.
Callable and Future.example: A background calculation can return its result later through a Future.
points_to_remember: Callable can return a value.
Callable can throw checked exceptions.
Future represents a pending or completed result.
get() retrieves the result and may block until completion.

Concurrent Collections.explanation: Concurrent collections are designed to support safe and efficient access by multiple threads.
Concurrent Collections.example: ConcurrentHashMap can be used when multiple threads need to access and modify a map concurrently.
points_to_remember: ConcurrentHashMap supports concurrent access.
Concurrent collections are designed for multithreaded programs.
They can be preferable to manually synchronizing an entire collection.
Other examples include CopyOnWriteArrayList and BlockingQueue.

Deadlock.explanation: A deadlock occurs when two or more threads wait indefinitely for resources held by each other, preventing all involved threads from continuing.
Deadlock.example: Thread A holds Resource 1 and waits for Resource 2, while Thread B holds Resource 2 and waits for Resource 1.
points_to_remember: Deadlocks can cause threads to wait indefinitely.
Consistent lock ordering can help prevent deadlocks.
Avoid unnecessary nested locks.
Careful synchronization design is important in concurrent programs.

Atomic Variables.explanation: Atomic classes provide thread-safe operations on individual variables without requiring traditional synchronized blocks for many common operations.
Atomic Variables.example: AtomicInteger can be used for safely incrementing a shared counter across multiple threads.
points_to_remember: Atomic classes support thread-safe operations.
AtomicInteger is useful for shared counters.
Atomic operations are designed for concurrent access.
Common classes include AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, and AtomicBoolean.

summary: Multithreading allows multiple threads to execute concurrently.
Threads can be created using Thread, Runnable, and higher-level concurrency APIs.
Synchronization helps protect shared mutable data.
Race conditions occur when concurrent access produces timing-dependent results.
ExecutorService simplifies thread and task management.
Concurrent collections provide thread-safe data structures.
Deadlocks occur when threads wait indefinitely for each other's resources.
Atomic classes provide thread-safe operations for common shared variables.
